title: Reversing a Linked List

concept: Given the head of a singly linked list, reverse the list so that the last node becomes the new head, and return it.

solutions.label: Copy to Array and Rebuild
solutions.summary: Store all values in an array, then build a new reversed list from the array.

solutions.label: Recursive Reversal
solutions.summary: Recursively reverse the rest of the list, then fix the pointers on the way back.

solutions.label: Iterative In-Place Reversal
solutions.summary: Use three pointers to reverse each link one node at a time in a single pass.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Here's the problem. You're given the head of a singly linked list. I'd like you to reverse the entire list and return the new head.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Understood. So if the list is one, two, three, four, the output should be four, three, two, one, correct?

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Exactly. The node that was last becomes the new head.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: A few clarifying questions. Can the list be empty or have just one node? And should I reverse it in place or can I create a new list?

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Yes, the list can be empty or contain a single node. In those cases just return the head as is. You may use any approach you like.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Got it. So I need to handle empty and single-node lists as edge cases, and for everything else, reverse the pointers so the last node becomes the head. Let me start with a straightforward approach.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: My first idea is simple. I'll traverse the list and copy every value into an array list. Then I'll build a new linked list by reading the array in reverse order.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: That works. What's the complexity?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Time is O of n because I visit each node twice, once to read and once to rebuild. Space is also O of n for the array and the new list.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Good analysis. This creates extra nodes though. Can you think of a way that reuses the existing nodes?

        R1["reverse(1)"] --> R2["reverse(2)"] --> R3["reverse(3)"] --> R4["reverse(4) base case"]
    end
    subgraph Unwind["Unwind and fix pointers"]
        U4[4] -->|"set 4.next = 3"| U3[3] -->|"set 3.next = 2"| U2[2] -->|"set 2.next = 1"| U1[1] -->|"set 1.next = null"| N[null]
    end
    Recurse --> Unwind
    style R1 fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    style R2 fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff

    style R4 fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: I can solve this recursively. The idea is to recurse all the way to the last node. That becomes the new head. Then as the recursion unwinds, I set each node's next pointer to point back to the current node.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: For our example, I recurse through one, two, three, four. Node four is the base case and becomes the new head. Then as we return, I set four's next to three, three's next to two, two's next to one, and finally one's next to null.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Nice. What about complexity now?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Time is O of n since we visit every node once. But space is still O of n because the recursion uses the call stack, which goes n levels deep.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Right. The call stack is a hidden cost. Can you eliminate that extra space?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The optimal way is iterative with three pointers: previous, current, and next. I start with previous as null and current at the head.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: At each step, I save current's next node, then point current's next to previous. Then I move previous to current, and current to the saved next node. I repeat until current is null.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Walking through our list: one, two, three, four. First, I redirect one's next from two to null. Then two's next from three to one. Then three's next from four to two. Then four's next from null to three. Now previous points to four, which is our new head.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: And the complexity?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Time is O of n for the single pass. Space is O of one because I only use three pointer variables regardless of list size.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Great job. You showed three approaches. The array copy is simple but uses extra space. Recursion is elegant but costs stack space. The iterative three-pointer method is the best, running in O of n time with O of one space.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The key insight is that we don't need to move data at all. We just redirect each pointer to the previous node. That pattern of previous, current, and next comes up in many linked list problems.
